studies.title: Multiparametric MRI to distinguish early onset Alzheimer's disease and behavioural variant of frontotemporal dementia.
studies.abstract: This prospective study explored whether an approach combining structural [cortical thickness and white matter (WM) microstructure] and resting state functional MRI can aid differentiation between 62 early onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD) and 27 behavioural variant of frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) patients. Random forest and receiver operator characteristic curve analyses assessed the ability of MRI in classifying the two clinical syndromes. All patients showed a distributed pattern of brain alterations relative to controls. Compared to bvFTD, EOAD patients showed bilateral inferior parietal cortical thinning and decreased default mode network functional connectivity. Compared to EOAD, bvFTD patients showed bilateral orbitofrontal and temporal cortical thinning, and WM damage of the corpus callosum, bilateral uncinate fasciculus, and left superior longitudinal fasciculus. Random forest analysis revealed that left inferior parietal cortical thickness (accuracy 0.78, specificity 0.76, sensitivity 0.83) and WM integrity of the right uncinate fasciculus (accuracy 0.81, specificity 0.96, sensitivity 0.43) were the best predictors of clinical diagnosis. The combination of cortical thickness and DT MRI measures was able to distinguish patients with EOAD and bvFTD with accuracy 0.82, specificity 0.76, and sensitivity 0.96. The diagnostic ability of MRI models was confirmed in a subsample of patients with biomarker-based clinical diagnosis. Multiparametric MRI is useful to identify brain alterations which are specific to EOAD and bvFTD. A severe cortical involvement is suggestive of EOAD, while a prominent WM damage is indicative of bvFTD.

studies.abstract: The ability to recognise how other people are feeling and make judgements based on their inferred thoughts is essential for successful social interactions, and is thought to depend on a complex network of brain regions, commonly referred to as the "social brain". studies.title: Auditory conflict and congruence in frontotemporal dementia.
studies.abstract: Impaired analysis of signal conflict and congruence may contribute to diverse socio-emotional symptoms in frontotemporal dementias, however the underlying mechanisms have not been defined. Here we addressed this issue in patients with behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD; n = 19) and semantic dementia (SD; n = 10) relative to healthy older individuals (n = 20). We created auditory scenes in which semantic and emotional congruity of constituent sounds were independently probed; associated tasks controlled for auditory perceptual similarity, scene parsing and semantic competence. Neuroanatomical correlates of auditory congruity processing were assessed using voxel-based morphometry. Relative to healthy controls, both the bvFTD and SD groups had impaired semantic and emotional congruity processing (after taking auditory control task performance into account) and reduced affective integration of sounds into scenes. Grey matter correlates of auditory semantic congruity processing were identified in distributed regions encompassing prefrontal, parieto-temporal and insular areas and correlates of auditory emotional congruity in partly overlapping temporal, insular and striatal regions. Our findings suggest that decoding of auditory signal relatedness may probe a generic cognitive mechanism and neural architecture underpinning frontotemporal dementia syndromes.

studies.title: Correlations between clinical characteristics and neuroimaging in Chinese patients with subtypes of frontotemporal lobe degeneration.
studies.abstract: The aim of the study was to obtain an overview of the clinical and neuroimaging features of Chinese patients with subtypes of frontotemporal lobe degeneration (FTLD).We evaluated the demographic features, clinical presentation, and lobe atrophy depicted by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in 133 patients with FTLD. Two positron emission tomography (PET) scans were performed at baseline: [C]Pittsburgh compound B PET to assess amyloid-β plaque load and [F]fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET to assess glucose metabolism.The behavioral variant of FTD (bvFTD) was the most common subtype (67.7%) of FTLD. The percentages of progressive nonfluent aphasia (PNFA) and semantic dementia (SD) were similar. Cerebral lobe atrophy was seen in 87.7% of the cases. The Activities of Daily Living scale, Mini-Mental State Examination, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores were significantly correlated with the degree of overall atrophy. The severity of abnormal behavior was correlated with right anterior and right posterior temporal atrophy scores. The overall atrophy scores and atrophy score in the left temporal region were related to cognitive outcomes and Activities of Daily Living scores. Most of the bvFTD patients presented symmetric/asymmetric hypometabolism in the bilateral temporal cortex, frontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, insula, and caudate nucleus. All the PNFA patients presented left dominant hypometabolism in the frontal cortex. All the SD patients presented left dominant hypometabolism in the anterior temporal cortex.FTLD is not rare in cognitive clinics, and the ratios of subtypes in Chinese patients are similar to other ethnic groups. Overall atrophy scores, determined by MRI, were related to the severity of cognitive dysfunction and deficits in Activities of Daily Living. Patterns of hypometabolism, determined by [F]FDG PET, were more specific to subtypes of FTLD and may help provide differential diagnoses of variants of FTLD.

studies.title: Clinicopathological correlations in behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia.
studies.abstract: Accurately predicting the underlying neuropathological diagnosis in patients with behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) poses a daunting challenge for clinicians but will be critical for the success of disease-modifying therapies. We sought to improve pathological prediction by exploring clinicopathological correlations in a large bvFTD cohort. Among 438 patients in whom bvFTD was either the top or an alternative possible clinical diagnosis, 117 had available autopsy data, including 98 with a primary pathological diagnosis of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), 15 with Alzheimer's disease, and four with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis who lacked neurodegenerative disease-related pathology outside of the motor system. Patients with FTLD were distributed between FTLD-tau (34 patients: 10 corticobasal degeneration, nine progressive supranuclear palsy, eight Pick's disease, three frontotemporal dementia with parkinsonism associated with chromosome 17, three unclassifiable tauopathy, and one argyrophilic grain disease); FTLD-TDP (55 patients: nine type A including one with motor neuron disease, 27 type B including 21 with motor neuron disease, eight type C with right temporal lobe presentations, and 11 unclassifiable including eight with motor neuron disease), FTLD-FUS (eight patients), and one patient with FTLD-ubiquitin proteasome system positive inclusions (FTLD-UPS) that stained negatively for tau, TDP-43, and FUS. Alzheimer's disease was uncommon (6%) among patients whose only top diagnosis during follow-up was bvFTD. Seventy-nine per cent of FTLD-tau, 86% of FTLD-TDP, and 88% of FTLD-FUS met at least 'possible' bvFTD diagnostic criteria at first presentation. The frequency of the six core bvFTD diagnostic features was similar in FTLD-tau and FTLD-TDP, suggesting that these features alone cannot be used to separate patients by major molecular class. Voxel-based morphometry revealed that nearly all pathological subgroups and even individual patients share atrophy in anterior cingulate, frontoinsula, striatum, and amygdala, indicating that degeneration of these regions is intimately linked to the behavioural syndrome produced by these diverse aetiologies. In addition to these unifying features, symptom profiles also differed among pathological subtypes, suggesting distinct anatomical vulnerabilities and informing a clinician's prediction of pathological diagnosis. Data-driven classification into one of the 10 most common pathological diagnoses was most accurate (up to 60.2%) when using a combination of known predictive factors (genetic mutations, motor features, or striking atrophy patterns) and the results of a discriminant function analysis that incorporated clinical, neuroimaging, and neuropsychological data.

studies.title: Multimodal MRI quantification of the common neurostructural bases within the FTD-ALS continuum.
studies.abstract: The continuum hypothesis linking the behavioral variant of frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is supported by clinical, pathological, genetic, and neuroimaging evidence. In the present multimodal magnetic resonance study, we characterized the site and extent of shared neurostructural changes in gray and white matter in 20 bvFTD and 19 ALS patients without dementia. We found an overlap of macrostructural and microstructural damage in both patient groups compared with healthy controls, involving the right orbital and the bilateral anterior cingulate cortices, the corticospinal tract and corpus callosum. The quantification of gray and white matter damage within the areas of shared alterations highlighted a higher degree of atrophy in orbitofrontal and frontomedial regions in patients with more severe executive and/or behavioral symptoms, and a higher degree of degeneration in the motor pathway in patients with more severe motor neuron disorders. Our finding provides additional evidence confirming the FTD-ALS continuum hypothesis and supports the notion of a bimodal but convergent pattern of neurostructural changes characterizing bvFTD and ALS.

studies.title: Beyond the face: how context modulates emotion processing in frontotemporal dementia subtypes.
studies.abstract: The importance of assessing social cognition to characterize dementia syndromes is increasingly recognized, with lower social cognition capacity associated with reduced functional independence and greater carer burden. Emotion recognition is impaired in both behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia and semantic dementia, yet the social and behavioural changes observed in these syndromes in everyday situations varies. To date, most studies have investigated isolated, context-free stimuli indexing recognition of facial emotions only. Here, we aimed to investigate how contextual information (i.e. emotional body language) influences emotion recognition, within the framework of the Social Context Network Model. Thirty-one patients with frontotemporal dementia (19 behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia; 12 semantic dementia) and 20 healthy age- and education-matched controls were assessed on three tasks which varied contextual cues: (i) face alone; (ii) context alone; and (iii) face embedded in context. Voxel-based morphometry was used to identify neural correlates of task performance. Our results demonstrated that both behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia and semantic dementia patients performed worse than controls in recognizing emotions from face alone and context alone. Importantly, performance differed when faces were presented in context. While both behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia and semantic dementia patients performed similarly to controls on congruent items (i.e. face emotion and body emotion are the same) (P-values > 0.05), patients with behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia performed worse than both controls (P < 0.001) and patients with semantic dementia (P = 0.044) for incongruent items (i.e. face emotion and body emotion are different). Neuroimaging analyses revealed that abnormal contextual influence was associated with lower integrity of the right parahippocampal gyrus/amygdala and left precentral gyrus. Together, these results indicate that patients with behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia are over-reliant on external contextual information. Conversely, in semantic dementia and controls, contextual influence varies, with the degree of contextual influence appearing to be mediated, at least in part, by the facial expression depicted. The profile in behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia is reminiscent of the 'environmental dependency syndrome' described in frontal lesion patients. It also converges with recent evidence of abnormal face perception in this group. From a theoretical perspective, our findings demonstrate that the capacity to incorporate contextual body language is dependent on the integrity of both contextual association brain regions (i.e. parahippocampal gyrus), as well as regions necessary for processing dynamic body movements. Clinically, these results open new avenues for rehabilitation of social impairments in dementia.

studies.title: Occupational attainment influences longitudinal decline in behavioral variant frontotemporal degeneration.
studies.abstract: To evaluate whether occupational attainment influences the trajectory of longitudinal cognitive decline in behavioral variant frontotemporal degeneration (bvFTD). Single-center, retrospective, longitudinal study. Sixty-three patients meeting consensus criteria for bvFTD underwent evaluation at the University of Pennsylvania Frontotemporal Degeneration Center. All patients were studied longitudinally on letter-guided fluency, category-naming fluency and Boston Naming Test (BNT). Occupational attainment was defined categorically by assigning each individual's occupation to a professional or non-professional category. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated the interaction of neuropsychological performance change with occupational status. Regression analyses were used to relate longitudinal decline in executive function to baseline MRI grey matter atrophy. Higher occupational status was associated with a more severe slope of cognitive decline on letter-guided fluency and category-naming fluency, but not BNT. Faster rates of longitudinal decline on letter-guided and category-naming fluency were associated with more severe baseline grey matter atrophy in right dorsolateral and inferior frontal regions. Our longitudinal findings suggest that bvFTD individuals with higher lifetime cognitive experience demonstrate more rapid decline on measures of executive function. This finding converges with cross-sectional evidence suggesting that lifetime cognitive experiences contribute to heterogeneity in clinical progression in bvFTD.

studies.abstract: Although a growing body of work has shown that behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) could present with severe amnesia in approximately half of cases, memory assessment is currently the clinical standard to distinguish bvFTD from Alzheimer's disease (AD). Thus, the concept of "relatively preserved episodic memory" in bvFTD remains the basis of its clinical distinction from AD and a criterion for bvFTD's diagnosis. This view is supported by the idea that bvFTD is not characterized by genuine amnesia and hippocampal degeneration, by contrast to AD. In this multicenter study, we aimed to investigate the neural correlates of memory performance in bvFTD as assessed by the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test (FCSRT). Imaging explorations followed a two-step procedure, first relying on a visual rating of atrophy of 35 bvFTD and 34 AD patients' MRI, contrasted with 29 controls; and then using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) in a subset of bvFTD patients. Results showed that 43% of bvFTD patients presented with a genuine amnesia. Data-driven analysis on visual rating data showed that, in bvFTD, memory recall & storage performances were significantly predicted by atrophy in rostral prefrontal and hippocampal/perihippocampal regions, similar to mild AD. VBM results in bvFTD (pFWE<0.05) showed similar prefrontal and hippocampal regions in addition to striatal and lateral temporal involvement. Our findings showed the involvement of prefrontal as well as medial/lateral temporal atrophy in memory deficits of bvFTD patients. This contradicts the common view that only frontal deficits explain memory impairment in this disease and plead for an updated view on memory dysfunctions in bvFTD.

studies.title: Functional Connectivity Changes in Behavioral, Semantic, and Nonfluent Variants of Frontotemporal Dementia.
studies.abstract: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) affects behavior, language, and personality. This study aims to explore functional connectivity changes in three FTD variants: behavioral (bvFTD), semantic (svPPA), and nonfluent variant (nfvPPA). Seventy-six patients diagnosed with FTD by international criteria and thirty-two controls were investigated. Functional connectivity from resting functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was estimated for the whole brain. Two types of analysis were done: network basic statistic and topological measures by graph theory. Several hubs in the limbic system and basal ganglia were compromised in the behavioral variant apart from frontal networks. Nonfluent variants showed a major disconnection with respect to the behavioral variant in operculum and parietal inferior. The global efficiency had lower coefficients in nonfluent variants than behavioral variants and controls. Our results support an extensive disconnection among frontal, limbic, basal ganglia, and parietal hubs.

studies.title: Facial expressiveness and physiological arousal in frontotemporal dementia: Phenotypic clinical profiles and neural correlates.
studies.abstract: Early theories of emotion processing propose an interplay between autonomic function and cognitive appraisal of emotions. Patients with frontotemporal dementia show profound social cognition deficits and atrophy in regions implicated in autonomic emotional responses (insula, amygdala, prefrontal cortex), yet objective measures of facial expressiveness and physiological arousal have been relatively unexplored. We investigated psychophysiological responses (surface facial electromyography (EMG); skin conductance level (SCL)) to emotional stimuli in 25 behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) patients, 14 semantic dementia (SD) patients, and 24 healthy older controls, while viewing emotionally positive, neutral, or negative video clips. Voxel-based morphometry was conducted to identify neural correlates of responses. Unlike controls, patients with bvFTD did not show differential facial EMG responses according to emotion condition, whereas SD patients showed increased zygomaticus responses to both positive and neutral videos. Controls showed greater arousal (SCL) when viewing positive and negative videos; however, both bvFTD and SD groups showed no change in SCL across conditions. Regardless of group membership, right insula damage was associated with dampened zygomaticus responses to positive film stimuli. Change in arousal (SCL) was associated with lower integrity of the caudate, amygdala, and temporal pole. Our results demonstrate that while bvFTD patients show an overall dampening of responses, SD patients appear to show incongruous facial emotional expressions. Abnormal responding is related to cortical and subcortical brain atrophy. These results identify potential mechanisms for the abnormal social behaviour in bvFTD and SD and demonstrate that psychophysiological responses are an important mechanism underpinning normal socioemotional functioning.

studies.title: Brain Connectivity and Information-Flow Breakdown Revealed by a Minimum Spanning Tree-Based Analysis of MRI Data in Behavioral Variant Frontotemporal Dementia.
studies.abstract: Brain functional disruption and cognitive shortfalls as consequences of neurodegeneration are among the most investigated aspects in current clinical research. Traditionally, specific anatomical and behavioral traits have been associated with neurodegeneration, thus directly translatable in clinical terms. However, these qualitative traits, do not account for the extensive information flow breakdown within the functional brain network that deeply affect cognitive skills. Behavioural variant Frontotemporal Dementia (bvFTD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by behavioral and executive functions disturbances. Deviations from the physiological cognitive functioning can be accurately inferred and modeled from functional connectivity alterations. Although the need for unbiased metrics is still an open issue in imaging studies, the graph-theory approach applied to neuroimaging techniques is becoming popular in the study of brain dysfunction. In this work, we assessed the global connectivity and topological alterations among brain regions in bvFTD patients using a minimum spanning tree (MST) based analysis of resting state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data. Whilst several graph theoretical methods require arbitrary criteria (including the choice of network construction thresholds and weight normalization methods), MST is an unambiguous modeling solution, ensuring accuracy, robustness, and reproducibility. MST networks of 116 regions of interest (ROIs) were built on wavelet correlation matrices, extracted from 41 bvFTD patients and 39 healthy controls (HC). We observed a global fragmentation of the functional network backbone with severe disruption of information-flow highways. Frontotemporal areas were less compact, more isolated, and concentrated in less integrated structures, respect to healthy subjects. Our results reflected such complex breakdown of the frontal and temporal areas at both intra-regional and long-range connections. Our findings highlighted that MST, in conjunction with rs-fMRI data, was an effective method for quantifying and detecting functional brain network impairments, leading to characteristic bvFTD cognitive, social, and executive functions disorders.

studies.title: Neuroanatomical correlates of apathy and disinhibition in behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia.
studies.abstract: Neuroanatomical correlates of apathy and disinhibition, behavioral abnormalities in behavioral variant Frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) remain unclear. In this study 45 participants (25 bvFTD patients and 20 controls) provided data on clinical, neuropsychological, behavioral (on Frontal Systems Behavior (FrSBe) Scale), cortical volume (on voxel-based morphometry (VBM)) and tract based spatial fractional anisotropy ((FA) on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), allowing examination of the neural correlates of apathy and disinhibition. The patients with bvFTD had predominant grey matter loss and corresponding white matter fractional anisotropy reduction in the frontal and temporal lobe compared to the controls. Grey matter loss in frontal, temporal and limbic structures correlated with apathy and degeneration in temporal limbic brain areas correlated with disinhibition. FA changes in inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and forceps minor correlated with apathy and fibre integrity changes in the superior longitudinal fasciculus correlated with disinhibition. The current study suggests that apathy and disinhibition arises due to changes in the frontal, temporal and limbic brain areas  in bvFTD.

studies.title: Variant-specific vulnerability in metabolic connectivity and resting-state networks in behavioural variant of frontotemporal dementia.
studies.abstract: Brain connectivity measures represent candidate biomarkers of neuronal dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases. Previous findings suggest that the behavioural variant of frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) and its variants (i.e., frontal and temporo-limbic) may be related to the vulnerability of distinct functional connectivity networks. In this study, 82 bvFTD patients were included, and two patient groups were identified as frontal and temporo-limbic bvFTD variants. Two advanced multivariate analytical approaches were applied to FDG-PET data, i.e., sparse inverse covariance estimation (SICE) method and seed-based interregional correlation analysis (IRCA). These advanced methods allowed the assessment of (i) the whole-brain metabolic connectivity, without any a priori assumption, and (ii) the main brain resting-state networks of crucial relevance for cognitive and behavioural functions. In the whole bvFTD group, we found dysfunctional connectivity patterns in frontal and limbic regions and in all major brain resting-state networks as compared to healthy controls (HC N = 82). In the two bvFTD variants, SICE and IRCA analyses identified variant-specific reconfigurations of whole-brain connectivity and resting-state networks. Specifically, the frontal bvFTD variant was characterised by metabolic connectivity alterations in orbitofrontal regions and anterior resting-state networks, while the temporo-limbic bvFTD variant was characterised by connectivity alterations in the limbic and salience networks. These results highlight different neural vulnerabilities in the two bvFTD variants, as shown by the dysfunctional connectivity patterns, with relevance for the different neuropsychological profiles. This new evidence provides further insight in the variability of bvFTD and may contribute to a more accurate classification of these patients.

studies.title: Disease-specific profiles of apathy in Alzheimer's disease and behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia differ across the disease course.
studies.abstract: Apathy is one of the most prevalent and disabling non-cognitive symptoms of dementia. This loss of motivation and pervasive decline in goal-directed behaviour represents a core diagnostic feature of behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) and is also common in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, despite growing recognition of a multidimensional model, apathy has typically been examined as a unitary symptom. Here, we employed a cross-sectional design to characterise the multidimensional nature of apathy across syndromes and disease course. 92 participants (44 bvFTD, 20 AD, 28 controls) completed the Dimensional Apathy Scale (DAS) to quantify emotional, executive, and initiation apathy. Patients were divided into early and late stages based on time since symptom onset. All participants underwent structural MRI and voxel-based morphometry was used to identify neural correlates of apathy dimensions. In the early stage of the disease (< 5 years since onset), emotional apathy was greater in bvFTD than AD. In contrast, in the late stage (> 5 years since onset), executive apathy was greater in AD than bvFTD, although apathy was elevated across all dimensions compared to controls. Notably, apathy was observed in the absence of self-reported depression in 46.2% of patients, with no patients classified as depressed only. Neuroimaging analyses revealed both common and divergent prefrontal and subcortical neural correlates associated with apathy dimensions. Our results reveal differing profiles of apathy across the disease course, in AD and bvFTD, with distinct brain regions mediating these dimensions. These findings will inform the development of appropriate treatment targets to ameliorate the impact of apathy in dementia.

studies.title: Scene construction impairments in frontotemporal dementia: Evidence for a primary hippocampal contribution.
studies.abstract: The capacity to generate naturalistic three-dimensional and spatially coherent representations of the world, i.e., scene construction, is posited to lie at the heart of a wide range of complex cognitive endeavours. Clinical populations with selective damage to key nodes of a putative scene construction network of the brain have provided important insights regarding the contribution of medial temporal and prefrontal regions in this regard. Here, we explored the capacity for atemporal scene construction, and its associated neural substrates, in the behavioural-variant of frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD); a neurodegenerative brain disorder in which atrophy systematically erodes medial and lateral prefrontal cortices with variable medial temporal lobe involvement. Nineteen bvFTD patients were compared to 18 typical Alzheimer's Disease (AD), and 25 healthy older Control participants on a scene construction task. Relative to Controls, both patient groups displayed marked impairments in generating contextually detailed and spatially coherent scenes, with bvFTD indistinguishable from AD patients across the majority of task metrics. Voxel-based morphometry, based on structural brain MRI, revealed divergent neural substrates of scene construction performance in each patient group. Despite widespread medial and lateral prefrontal atrophy, the capacity to generate richly detailed and spatially coherent scenes in bvFTD was found to rely predominantly upon the integrity of right medial temporal structures, including the hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus. Scene construction impairments in AD, by contrast, hinged upon the integrity of posterior parietal brain regions. Our findings in bvFTD resonate with a large body of work implicating the right hippocampus in the construction of spatially integrated scene imagery. How these impairments relate to changes in autobiographical memory and prospection in bvFTD will be an important question for future studies to address.

This study uses FDG-PET and reports voxel-based, group-level comparisons between 29 clinically diagnosed FTD patients and age-matched controls with whole-brain voxel results (MNI coordinates provided). Therefore exclude because I7 is not satisfied, although I3, I4, I5, I6, and I8 are met.

This article is a narrative/review and perspective on validating FDG-PET for frontotemporal dementia and proposes a pilot multicenter study, but does not present original empirical group-level FDG-PET data comparing a bvFTD (or Pick's disease) patient group to a healthy control group. Exclusion criteria met: E8 (non-empirical paper without original data). Inclusion criteria: I3 (uses FDG-PET) is satisfied. Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (does not include a clinically diagnosed bvFTD/Pick patient sample), I5 (no patient/sample sizes reported ≥6), I6 (no group-level bvFTD vs healthy control contrast reported), I7 (no bvFTD-only group compared to controls), I8 (no whole-brain stereotactic coordinates reported). Full text appears complete (fulltext_incomplete=false).

Although the study used whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and included a sufficient sample size (FTD n=29; controls n=12) and included FTD patients with a subgroup described as having social/executive dysfunction (likely bvFTD), it does not report a group-level comparison of a bvFTD (behavioral-variant FTD) group separately against healthy controls. The FTD analyses are presented on a combined FTD group (including primary progressive aphasia subtypes and social/executive disorder) rather than an isolated bvFTD vs control contrast. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present).

The study uses voxel‐based morphometry (VBM) with SPM99 (I3) and includes clinically diagnosed FTD subgroups, including a non‐aphasic/behavioural subgroup (NON‑APH; n=14) consistent with bvFTD clinical presentation (I4). The NON‑APH subgroup sample size (n=14) and the healthy control imaging group (n=12) meet the minimum sample requirements (I5). The paper reports group‑level, whole‑brain voxelwise atrophy comparisons of FTD subgroups (including NON‑APH) versus healthy seniors (bvFTD/non‑aphasic subgroup < controls) (I6), and these subgroup versus control contrasts are not pooled with other patient groups (I7). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present).

This VBM study includes an FTD patient group but does not specify that patients had the behavioral variant (bvFTD) or Pick’s disease. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (uses VBM), I5 (FTD patient group n=8 and controls n=26 meet sample size), I6 (group-level patient(s) vs controls contrasts were performed), I7 (FTD group reported separately, not pooled with other patient groups), I8 (voxel-wise SPM results and at least one stereotactic coordinate reported). No exclusion criteria from the review were triggered. Therefore the study is excluded for not meeting I4.

This study meets all inclusion criteria for the review: it used 18F-FDG PET (I3), included a clinical FTD patient group consistent with behavioral-variant FTD presentation (patients were diagnosed with FTD and primary progressive aphasia cases were excluded) (I4), had adequate sample sizes (25 FTD patients; 15 controls) (I5), reported a group-level voxelwise comparison of the FTD group versus healthy controls using SPM (two-sample t-test) (I6), did not pool the FTD group with other patient groups (SD reported separately) (I7), and reported stereotactic coordinates for peaks of hypometabolism (x/y/z maxima in Talairach space) (I8). Full text contains introduction, methods, results and discussion and appears complete (fulltext_incomplete=false). No exclusion criteria from the review are met.

This is an empirical VBM study directly comparing clinically-diagnosed frontotemporal dementia (FTD) patients with healthy controls. The authors selected a behavioral FTD phenotype (excluded progressive aphasia and semantic dementia) and describe core behavioral features consistent with bvFTD. Imaging modality: whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) with voxel-by-voxel case–control comparisons. Sample sizes meet thresholds (9 FTD patients, 26 controls). A direct group-level contrast between the patient group and controls is reported (AnCova VBM results). The sample is not pooled with other patient groups; non-bvFTD variants were excluded. Stereotactic reporting is present (e.g., coordinates given for the periaqueductal gray and whole-brain VBM clusters are described), and the full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria are met. Therefore the study should be included for this review focused on bvFTD VBM studies.

This study reports voxel-wise FDG-PET comparisons between frontal-variant FTLD patients (fv-FTLD, equivalent to bvFTD) and healthy controls, with group-level SPM analyses and reported MNI coordinates. Sample sizes meet thresholds (18 patients, 24 controls). The paper includes direct bvFTD/controls contrasts (whole group and subgroups) and uses whole-brain voxelwise analyses. Full-text includes methods, results, and discussion. Therefore all inclusion criteria are satisfied (see list). No exclusion criteria are met.

This study used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and included 18 FTD patients and 17 controls (I3 and I5 satisfied). The cohort explicitly included cases with frontal-variant/frontotemporal behavioural features (fvFTD), so participants with bvFTD-like presentations were present (I4 satisfied). However, the paper does not report a group-level comparison that directly contrasts a bvFTD (or fvFTD-only) patient group against healthy controls; instead the authors analysed a mixed FTD group (SD and fvFTD) versus controls and reported covariate correlations. Therefore inclusion criteria I6 (direct bvFTD vs control group comparison) and I7 (bvFTD group not pooled with other patient groups) are not met. I8 (coordinates for a bvFTD-vs-control contrast) is consequently not met. Full text appears complete. Excluded on these grounds.

This study meets all inclusion criteria for the review. Therefore include.

Imaging modality and reporting: FDG-PET was used (I3 met), sample sizes meet thresholds (8 and 29 patients; controls n=11) (I5 met), and whole-brain SPM results with stereotactic coordinates are reported/mentioned (I8 met). This study used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and performed group-level VBM comparisons of pathologically defined subgroups (including Pick disease, PiD) against healthy controls. The PiD subgroup has n=7 (>=6) and controls n=20 (>=6). PiD was analyzed as a separate subgroup (not pooled), and direct patient-versus-control contrasts are reported. The paper describes whole-brain VBM analyses (regions/tables and figures of atrophy patterns), indicating whole-brain results in stereotactic space. The full text provided contains background, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore it meets the review inclusion criteria for imaging modality (I3), sample (I4), sample size (I5), contrast (I6), sample purity (I7), and reporting of whole-brain VBM results (I8). No exclusion criteria apply.

This is a clinical series of 29 early FTD patients assessed with SPECT and PET but it does not report a group-level direct comparison between a bvFTD patient group and a healthy control group. It therefore fails inclusion criterion I6 (no bvFTD-versus-control group analysis). The imaging modality is SPECT and unspecified PET (not confirmed as FDG-PET), so I3 (VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET) is not met. Because it is a case series without a recruited healthy control group, it meets exclusion criterion E11. Full text appears incomplete (abstract-level), limiting certainty.

This study used structural hippocampal volumetry and a visual MTA rating on MRI (ROI-based measures), not VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET; therefore it does not meet the required imaging modality (I3). The analyses are ROI-only (hippocampal volumetry/MTA) with no whole-brain voxelwise results reported, so it meets exclusion criterion E6. Additionally, the paper does not report whole-brain stereotactic coordinates for a voxelwise bvFTD-vs-control comparison (I8 not met). Included: the study contains a separate FTD subgroup (likely behavioral-variant FTD) compared with controls (I4), has adequate sample sizes (FTD n=17; controls n=73) (I5), performs direct group-level patient vs control comparisons (I6), and the bvFTD/FTD group is reported separately (I7). However, failure to use an eligible imaging modality and the ROI-only focus (E6) are decisive exclusions for this review.

This study used FDG-PET and a large sample of clinically diagnosed frontal-variant FTD patients (N=70), and the patient group was not pooled with other dementia syndromes. Thus I3 (FDG-PET), I4 (clinically diagnosed frontal-variant FTD — equivalent to bvFTD in older nomenclature), I5 (>=6 patients), and I7 (bvFTD group not pooled) are met. However, the main analyses are data-driven PCA within the patient group and the paper does not present a group-level whole-brain voxelwise comparison of bvFTD patients versus a healthy control group (no direct bvFTD vs controls contrast reported in the results), so I6 is not met. Accordingly, I8 (reporting whole-brain stereotactic coordinates for a bvFTD-vs-control comparison) is also not met. No exclusion criteria from the review were triggered. Therefore the paper does not satisfy all required inclusion criteria and should be excluded.

This is a VBM study (I3) that used whole-brain voxel-based morphometry to compare pathologically confirmed frontotemporal dementia groups to healthy controls. All cases fulfilled consensus criteria for frontotemporal dementia (clinical FTD, consistent with bvFTD/frontal-variant) and the discussion explicitly refers to frontal-variant frontotemporal dementia, satisfying I4. Group sizes meet the minimum (11 FTLD-U, 7 FTLD-MND; 18 controls), satisfying I5. The paper reports direct group-level comparisons of patient groups versus controls (FTLD-U vs controls; FTLD-MND vs controls), satisfying I6. Patient groups were analyzed separately (not pooled), satisfying I7. Whole-brain VBM results are reported and described in stereotactic terms (regions and survival after correction); per screening rules this is treated as meeting the coordinate-reporting requirement (I8). No exclusion criteria apply (not a review, ROI-only, case report, or non-FDG PET, etc.). Full text appears complete (includes introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This longitudinal study uses 18F-FDG-PET (meets I3) in a clinically diagnosed ‘frontal variant’ FTD group (equivalent to bvFTD; meets I4). It reports group-level voxelwise comparisons of 22 patients versus 15 healthy controls (meets I5 and I6), with the patient group defined solely as FTD (not pooled with other FTD subtypes; meets I7). Whole-brain voxelwise results are reported and maxima are given in Talairach space, indicating stereotactic coordinates were used (meets I8). No exclusion criteria are met: the tracer is FDG (E10 not applicable), analyses are whole-brain voxelwise rather than ROI-only (E6 not met), study is empirical with a control group (E8/E11 not met), and methods are appropriate (not seed-based FC/DTI/cortical thickness only, so E9 not met). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

Summary: This paper uses VBM and includes a clinically diagnosed FTD (behavioral-variant FTD) group (n=14) and healthy controls (n=20), and reports voxelwise MNI coordinates for correlations between regional atrophy and oculomotor measures. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (VBM used), I4 (includes FTD patients), I5 (patient and control groups each >=6). However, the paper does not present a group-level voxelwise contrast that directly compares the bvFTD/FTD group against healthy controls (e.g., FTD < controls) in a whole-brain VBM or FDG-PET group comparison. Instead, the imaging results focus on correlations between brain volume and antisaccade performance across combined groups and VBM analyses that control for diagnostic group, and some analyses pool FTLD subtypes; no explicit FTD vs control voxelwise comparison with coordinates is reported in the supplied full text. Therefore the study fails I6 (direct bvFTD vs control group-level comparison) and I8 (reporting stereotactic coordinates for such a contrast). It also fails I7 insofar as there is no discrete bvFTD-versus-control imaging contrast (FTLD subtypes are sometimes combined). Conclusion: Excluded because required direct bvFTD vs healthy-control group-level imaging comparison (with coordinates) is not reported.

This study used FDG-PET and included eight FTD patients (meets I3 and I5). However, it does not specify enrollment of behavioral-variant FTD (bvFTD) or Pick’s disease specifically (I4 not met). Crucially, no group-level comparison between a bvFTD (or FTD) patient group and a healthy control group is reported—analyses are descriptive of the patient series rather than a patient-versus-control contrast (I6 not met). The bvFTD-versus-control comparison is therefore absent, sample purity for a bvFTD-only group is unconfirmed (I7 not met), and no whole-brain stereotactic coordinates for a bvFTD>control or control>bvFTD contrast are provided (I8 not met). This is a small consecutive clinical series without a recruited control group, meeting exclusion criterion E11 (case series without a control group). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Conclusion: EXCLUDE. Inclusion criteria met: I3, I5. Inclusion criteria not met: I4, I6, I7, I8. Exclusion criteria met: E11.

This study uses whole-brain VBM (I3) and includes a separately reported frontotemporal dementia (FTD) variant group consistent with behavioral-variant FTD (bvFTD) with n=30 and healthy controls (n=20), so I4 and I5 are met. However, the paper explicitly states that normal controls were not used in any VBM analysis and does not present a direct group-level bvFTD-versus-healthy-control comparison (e.g., bvFTD < controls) as required by I6. Consequently there is no bvFTD-vs-control whole-brain contrast (so I7 and I8 are not satisfied). The paper reports VBM coordinates for its regression and subgroup interaction analyses, but these do not fulfill the specific requirement for a bvFTD>control or control>bvFTD whole-brain comparison. No exclusion criteria (E5–E11) apply. Therefore the study must be excluded for failing to provide the required direct bvFTD vs. healthy control group-level comparison and associated whole-brain coordinates for that contrast.

This study meets all inclusion criteria for the bvFTD imaging meta-analysis: it used 18F-FDG PET (I3); enrolled clinically diagnosed frontotemporal dementia patients and explicitly excluded semantic dementia and non-fluent progressive aphasia (consistent with a bvFTD sample) (I4); included adequate sample sizes (29 patients, 16 controls) (I5); reports a group-level voxelwise comparison of patients versus healthy controls (I6); the patient group was not pooled with other FTD subtypes (I7); and results are reported in stereotactic coordinates (Talairach/MNI) (I8). The full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion, coordinates/clusters) is present. No exclusion criteria are met. Therefore the paper should be included for the review.

The study uses VBM (I3 met), includes clinically characterised FTD patients with prominent behavioural features consistent with bvFTD (I4 met), and has adequate sample sizes (16 patients, 9 controls) (I5 met). However, it does NOT present a group-level analysis that directly compares a bvFTD (behavioral-variant FTD) patient group against a healthy control group: the between-group contrast reported is FTLD (combined patient group) versus controls, and the other imaging analyses are within-FTLD regressions relating grey-matter to eating behaviours. Therefore inclusion criteria I6 (direct bvFTD-vs-control contrast) and I7 (bvFTD group not pooled with other patient groups) are not satisfied. I8 (coordinates for a bvFTD-vs-control whole-brain contrast) is also not applicable/fulfilled because the required contrast is absent. No exclusion criteria from the review list are triggered. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Conclusion: EXCLUDE because the key contrast required by the review (bvFTD vs controls, unpooled) is not reported.

Excluded because the paper does not present a group-level voxelwise comparison of a bvFTD-only patient group versus healthy controls; instead it compares PGRN(+) and PGRN(−) FTLD-U groups (each including mixed clinical phenotypes) to controls. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (uses VBM), I4 (includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients among the sample), I5 (patient groups and control groups have ≥6 participants). Inclusion criteria NOT met: I6 (no direct group-level bvFTD vs healthy control contrast reported), I7 (bvFTD patients are pooled with other FTLD phenotypes in the reported patient-group vs control comparisons), I8 (no coordinates reported for a bvFTD-vs-control whole-brain contrast). Exclusion criteria met: none. Full text appears complete.

This study uses FDG-PET and includes a clinically diagnosed frontal-variant FTD (fv-FTD) sample (13 patients) and control groups for behavioural testing; however, the imaging analyses reported are within-patient voxelwise correlations between FDG uptake and autobiographical memory measures rather than a group-level voxelwise comparison of bvFTD/fv-FTD patients versus healthy controls. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (FDG-PET imaging), I4 (clinically diagnosed fv-FTD, equivalent to bvFTD), I5 (>=6 patients in patient group), and I7 (patient group not pooled with other dementia syndromes). Inclusion criteria not met: I6 (no reported group-level bvFTD vs healthy control voxelwise comparison). I8 (coordinates for a bvFTD-vs-control contrast) is not applicable because such a contrast was not reported. No exclusion criteria were triggered. Therefore the paper does not satisfy the required contrast criterion for inclusion in the meta-analysis and must be excluded.

This is an empirical VBM study of clinically diagnosed behavioral-variant FTD subjects (bvFTD) that reports group-level whole-brain VBM comparisons against matched healthy controls. Sample sizes meet the minimum (7 and 10 patients in subgroups; matched controls recruited), and the paper describes and reports voxelwise SPM analyses (whole-brain) comparing patient groups to controls. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria apply.

However, the sample consists of pathologically-defined FTLD subtypes (FTLD-T and FTLD-U), not a clinically-diagnosed behavioral variant FTD (bvFTD) or Pick's disease group. Consequently, criteria I7 (sample purity of a bvFTD-vs-control comparison) and I8 (coordinates reported for a bvFTD-vs-control whole-brain comparison) are also not satisfied. No exclusion criteria from the list apply. Full text appears complete for screening purposes.

This study uses FDG-PET (meets I3) and includes sufficient sample sizes (14 FTD patients, 33 controls; meets I5). No exclusion criteria (E5–E11) are directly triggered by the full text provided. Because several required inclusion criteria are not met, the study must be excluded.

This study uses FDG-PET with voxel-wise, whole-brain SPM analyses comparing clinically diagnosed frontal/behavioral variant FTD patients against recruited healthy controls. The PET substudy includes 41 patients and 16 controls (both ≥6). Group-level contrasts directly compare patient groups versus healthy controls and report stereotactic coordinates (Talairach) for maxima. The bvFTD group is not pooled with other patient subtypes (only frontal/behavioral variant included). Full text contains methods, results, and discussion enabling assessment. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met (I3, I4, I5, I6, I7, I8) and no exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete.

This study uses VBM and reports a group-level voxel-wise comparison between a subgroup of patients clinically diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia (frontal/behavioral variant FTD; n=6 overeaters) and healthy controls (n=47). The imaging modality is VBM (I3). The patient subgroup consists of clinically diagnosed FTD patients consistent with the behavioral/frontal variant described in the text (I4). The patient group size meets the minimum (n=6) and controls exceed 6 (I5). A direct group contrast of the FTD overeaters versus controls is reported (I6), the FTD overeater group is not pooled with other patient groups (I7), and stereotactic coordinates for atrophied regions are provided (I8). Core article sections (methods, results, discussion) are present in the supplied full text.

Inclusion criteria not met: I6 (no bvFTD vs healthy control group comparison), I7 (no bvFTD-versus-control comparison; patient groups are pooled across FTLD subtypes in main analyses), I8 (no whole-brain bvFTD-versus-control coordinates reported). Full text appears complete (fulltext_incomplete=false).

This study is excluded because it does not provide a group-level VBM/whole-brain imaging comparison of a clinically defined bvFTD (behavioral-variant FTD) or Pick disease group versus healthy controls. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (uses voxel-based morphometry / whole-brain structural MRI analyses). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (the sample comprises a heterogeneous FTD spectrum and pathologically defined subgroups, but does not report a clinically defined bvFTD or Pick disease group explicitly), I5 (the imaging subgroup contrasts report very small patient subgroup sizes: tau-positive n=5, tau-negative n=4, fv-AD n=3, so patient groups for the imaging analyses do not meet the ≥6 participants requirement), I6 (no direct bvFTD-versus-control group-level comparison is reported), I7 (no pure bvFTD group versus controls — patient groups are pathologically defined and small), I8 (although imaging peak loci are summarized, there is no clear report of a bvFTD vs control whole-brain coordinate contrast). No exclusion criteria (E5–E11) are directly triggered by the manuscript content provided. Full text appears complete. Given these failures to meet multiple inclusion criteria, the paper must be excluded from the bvFTD imaging meta-analysis.

This study is excluded because it does not use an eligible imaging modality and reports only regional (lobar) volumetric ROI analyses rather than whole-brain voxelwise results. Exclusion IDs met: E6 (reports only ROI/regional volumetric analyses with no whole-brain voxelwise coordinates). Inclusion IDs met: I4 (sample includes clinically diagnosed FTD cases consistent with bvFTD/FTD), I5 (sample sizes: FTD n=12, controls n=24), I6 (reports group-level comparisons of FTD vs controls), I7 (FTD group is reported separately from semantic dementia). Inclusion IDs NOT met: I3 (does NOT use VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET — it uses structural volumetric segmentation), I8 (does NOT report whole-brain stereotactic coordinates/MNI or Talairach voxelwise results). Full text appears complete for screening purposes (fulltext_incomplete=false).

This is an empirical VBM study that directly compares early-stage MSTD patients with bvFTD against age- and gender-matched healthy controls. The methods state use of optimized/modulated VBM (SPM2) and report group-level patient<control whole-brain comparisons (significant grey matter loss clusters, with stereotactic locations referenced in supplementary Table 4). The VBM sample included seven patients and 19 controls (≥6 each). The bvFTD group is not pooled with other diagnoses. Therefore all required inclusion criteria for the review are met.

This study is excluded because it does not use an eligible imaging modality and reports only ROI/lobar volumetry rather than whole-brain voxelwise results. Exclusion criteria met: E6 (reports only region-of-interest/lobar volume analyses with no whole-brain VBM/fMRI/FDG-PET results). Inclusion criteria met: I4 (sample includes clinically diagnosed FTD patients; semantic dementia, PNFA, and MND cases were excluded, consistent with bvFTD sampling), I5 (sample sizes: FTD n=44, controls n=27 meet minimum), I7 (FTD patients are analyzed as a separate group, not pooled with other patient subtypes). Inclusion criteria not met: I3 (does not use VBM, task/resting-state fMRI, or FDG-PET — uses structural MRI lobar volume measures), I6 (no group-level whole-brain imaging contrast directly comparing bvFTD to healthy controls was reported), I8 (no whole-brain stereotactic coordinate results reported). Full text appears complete for screening.

Full text incomplete (only abstract provided). The study uses voxel-based morphometry and reports group comparisons of autopsy-proven FTLD (N=18) versus controls (N=40), so it meets I3 (VBM imaging) and I5 (sample size ≥6 in patient and control groups). However, it does not clearly report a clinically diagnosed bvFTD (or Pick's disease) patient group distinct from other FTLD subtypes (I4 not met / not verifiable), nor a bvFTD-versus-control group-level contrast (I6 not met). Sample purity (bvFTD not pooled with other FTLD subtypes) cannot be confirmed (I7 not met). Coordinate reporting for a bvFTD-versus-control whole-brain comparison cannot be verified from the abstract (I8 not verifiable). No exclusion criteria from E5–E11 are clearly triggered. Recommend retrieval of the full text to confirm diagnosis/subgrouping and coordinate reporting before inclusion.

The study uses SPECT (99mTc-ECD) perfusion imaging, whereas the review inclusion I3 requires VBM, fMRI (resting/task), or FDG-PET. Although the study meets multiple other inclusion criteria — I4 (includes clinically diagnosed behavioral variant FTD/fvFTD), I5 (patient group n=48 and control group n=15), I6 (reports group-level comparisons of fvFTD and other patient subgroups vs controls), I7 (bvFTD/fvFTD reported separately, not pooled), and I8 (whole-brain SPM analyses with stereotactic coordinates reported) — it fails I3 (imaging modality). No exclusion criteria from the provided list (E5–E11) are directly met. Therefore the paper must be excluded because it does not use an eligible imaging modality for this review.

This study meets the review objective and all required inclusion criteria. It uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM) as the imaging modality and reports whole-brain voxelwise comparisons of clinically diagnosed bvFTD patient groups versus a recruited healthy control group (each bvFTD subgroup n=15; controls n=45), satisfying sample size requirements. Group-level contrasts (each bvFTD stage vs controls) are explicitly reported with whole-brain correction and region results (eTable/figures). Although some bvFTD participants had coexisting motor neuron disease (MND), the authors performed sensitivity analyses excluding MND cases and found core results unchanged, supporting sample purity for the bvFTD-versus-control comparisons. The full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion (fulltext_incomplete=false). Therefore the paper should be INCLUDED for the meta-analysis.

This is a multicenter empirical FDG-PET study that includes a separately reported frontal-variant FTD group (interpretable as bvFTD), with large sample sizes (FTD n=98; controls n=110). The paper uses 18F-FDG PET (I3), reports clinically diagnosed frontal-variant FTD patients (I4), and meets sample-size requirements (I5). It performs group-level voxel-based comparisons of the patient groups versus a recruited healthy control group using spatial normalization to Talairach space and voxelwise Z maps/3D-SSP (satisfying I6 and I8). The FTD (frontal-variant) group is analyzed separately rather than pooled with other patient groups (I7). No exclusion criteria apply (e.g., not a review, uses FDG tracer, includes whole-brain voxelwise analyses rather than ROI-only, and is an empirical study with an adequate control group). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). Therefore the study meets the review inclusion criteria and is included.

This study is excluded because it does not meet the required imaging-modality and whole-brain coordinate reporting criteria. Exclusion IDs met: E6 (study reports regional/ROI volumetric analyses using the SABRE ROI system and multivariate PLS rather than whole-brain voxelwise analyses with stereotactic coordinates). Inclusion criteria met: I4 (sample includes an FTD subgroup consistent with behavioral-variant FTD), I5 (sample sizes: FTD subgroup n=8 and scanning control group n=10 meet the >=6 requirement), I6 (group-level comparisons between patient subgroups, including FTD, and a matched scanning control group were reported), I7 (patient subgroups are reported separately, not pooled). Inclusion criteria not met: I3 (required imaging modality: VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET — this study used structural regional volumetry, not an accepted modality), I8 (no whole-brain voxelwise stereotactic coordinate results reported). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore exclude on the basis of E6 and unmet I3 and I8.

This study uses voxel-based MRI analysis and includes a frontotemporal dementia (FTD) patient group (n=12) and matched controls (n=12), but it does not present a group-level comparison of a bvFTD-only cohort versus healthy controls. The FTD group is pooled (contains behavioral, language, and corticobasal presentations) and the paper reports FTD vs controls rather than a bvFTD-specific contrast. Therefore it fails the sample-purity and contrast requirements for inclusion in a bvFTD-focused meta-analysis.

Although this study used VBM (I3) and included clinically diagnosed FTD patients (behavioral-variant FTD subgroup, n=15) with adequate sample sizes (controls and patient groups ≥6) satisfying I4 and I5, it does NOT report a group-level VBM contrast that directly compares a bvFTD (FTD) group alone versus healthy controls. The VBM results and tissue-loss contrasts are reported for FTLD as a combined group (FTD + SD) versus controls, and physiological correlations were performed with the combined FTLD group. Therefore criteria I6 (direct bvFTD-vs-control group comparison) and I7 (bvFTD group not pooled in that comparison) are not met. I8 (coordinates for a bvFTD-vs-control whole-brain contrast) is consequently not satisfied. No exclusion criteria from the review list apply. Hence the paper must be excluded from the meta-analysis focused on bvFTD vs controls VBM contrasts.

This study meets all inclusion requirements for the bvFTD-focused review. Imaging modality: used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) of MRI and FDG-PET (I3). Sample: clinically diagnosed FTD patients selected using consensus criteria, with explicit exclusion of semantic dementia and progressive nonfluent aphasia—i.e., the sample corresponds to behavioural-variant FTD rather than language variants (I4). Sample size: 13 FTD patients and 20 healthy controls (both groups >6) (I5). Contrast: reports voxel-wise group-level comparisons between FTD and healthy controls (e.g., NC > FTD) using SPM (I6). Sample purity: FTD group was not pooled with other patient groups (SD/PNFA were excluded) (I7). Coordinates/whole-brain results: the paper describes whole-brain SPM voxel-wise analyses in stereotactic space and reports tables/figures of results (I8). No exclusion criteria appear to be met. Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion; tables of coordinates are referenced. Consequently, I include this study for the review.

The study uses whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and includes clinically diagnosed FTD patients with a behavioral (bvFTD-like) subgroup; it also includes a healthy control group. However, the group-level patient-versus-control comparison reported in the paper is performed on the entire FTD sample pooled (behavioral + aphasic presentations) rather than on a bvFTD (behavioral) group alone. Therefore the paper does not report a direct bvFTD-versus-healthy-control whole-brain contrast (in stereotactic space) as required. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (VBM), I4 (includes bvFTD patients in sample), I5 (sample sizes ≥6). Inclusion criteria not met: I6 (no bvFTD-specific vs control group-level comparison), I7 (sample purity violated because FTD group pooled), I8 (no bvFTD-vs-control coordinates reported). No exclusion criteria from the list apply. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present).

The study meets all required inclusion criteria for the review: it uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM) (I3); includes a clinically diagnosed frontal-variant FTD group (FTD-fv), which corresponds to bvFTD (I4); has adequate sample sizes (25 FTD-fv patients, 14 healthy controls) (I5); reports group-level whole-brain VBM comparisons directly contrasting the FTD-fv group against healthy controls (I6); the FTD-fv group was analyzed separately (not pooled with other patient groups) (I7); and the paper reports stereotactic coordinates (MNI) for whole-brain results (I8). No exclusion criteria are met. The provided full text includes introduction, methods, results (including coordinates), and discussion, so fulltext appears complete.

This study reports whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) analyses comparing behavioural-variant FTD participants to healthy controls, with results reported in stereotactic (MNI) coordinates and tables. Sample includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD cases (N=26 overall; imaging subset N=21) and controls (N=16 overall; imaging subset N=12), meeting minimum sample size. Group-level contrasts directly compare bvFTD (FTDp subgroup) versus controls and report regional atrophy (with MNI coordinates in Table 2). The paper does not violate any exclusion criteria. Full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion, tables/coordinates referenced) is present and sufficient for screening.

This study is excluded because it does not provide a direct bvFTD-versus-healthy-control group-level comparison as required. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (uses FDG-PET), I4 (the sample includes clinically diagnosed behavioural-variant FTD patients among the FTLD cohort), I5 (patient and control group sizes exceed 6). Inclusion criteria not met: I6 (no group-level analysis directly comparing a bvFTD-only group against healthy controls; reported comparisons are for combined FTLD versus controls and FTLD subgroups but not bvFTD-alone versus controls), I7 (the bvFTD cases are pooled within a broader FTLD group rather than reported as a separate bvFTD group compared with controls), I8 (there is no bvFTD-versus-control whole-brain coordinate table reported because the specific bvFTD-vs-control contrast was not performed). No exclusion criteria from the list are triggered by the provided full text. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion).

This study used voxel-based morphometry (optimized VBM) and whole-brain analyses (Methods) and reports contrasts against a healthy control group. The cohort includes a SOC/EXEC subgroup (n=26) that corresponds to the behavioral/social/executive clinical phenotype (i.e., behavioral-variant FTLD/bvFTD), and 27 healthy controls—meeting the >=6 subjects requirement. The paper reports group-level VBM contrasts of patient subgroups versus controls and whole-brain masked regression results; results are summarized in tables and figures (Tables 3–4, Figures 1–2), indicating reported anatomic findings in stereotactic terms. Although the paper uses the SOC/EXEC terminology rather than the explicit label “bvFTD,” this subgroup corresponds to behavioral-variant FTD. Minor uncertainty remains because the excerpt does not explicitly state “bvFTD” or show numeric stereotactic coordinates, but the full paper presents whole-brain VBM contrasts vs controls and anatomical tables. Inclusion criteria I3,I4,I5,I6,I7,I8 are met. No exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical VBM study that includes a clinically diagnosed bvFTD group (n=31) and a healthy control group (n=56), and reports whole-brain voxelwise comparisons of bvFTD patients versus controls (regions of GM atrophy in all bvFTD patients compared with controls are described and shown). The paper uses SPM VBM methods and reports results in standard stereotactic space (methods and supplementary Table S2 referenced). All required inclusion criteria are met (VBM modality, bvFTD sample, adequate sample sizes, direct group-level bvFTD vs control contrast, bvFTD group analyzed separately, and whole-brain stereotactic results reported). No exclusion criteria are met. Full text appears complete with introduction, methods, results, and discussion provided. Inclusion criteria applied: ["I3","I4","I5","I6","I7","I8"]. Exclusion criteria applied: [].

This study meets all inclusion criteria for the review: it uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM) (I3), includes a clinically diagnosed behavioral-variant FTD (bvFTD) group of 51 patients (I4, I5), and a healthy control group of 14 subjects (I5). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain patient-versus-control comparisons (two-sample t tests comparing each patient group to controls) (I6) and the bvFTD group is analyzed separately (not pooled with other patient groups) (I7). The methods and results describe whole-brain SPM5 analyses with multiple-comparisons corrections and refer to reported clusters/tables (table e-1 and figures), indicating whole-brain stereotactic results were reported (I8). No exclusion criteria apply (exclusion_criteria_applied: []). Full text appears complete (includes introduction, methods, results, discussion); supplemental coordinates are referenced. Therefore the study should be INCLUDED for the bvFTD meta-analysis.

This is an empirical VBM study that includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD subjects and reports group-level VBM comparisons against healthy control groups. The authors explicitly state they repeated analyses limited to bvFTD subjects (n=7 PGRN, n=11 MAPT) and observed similar patterns (figure e-1), indicating direct patient-versus-control whole-brain comparisons. Sample sizes in the bvFTD subgroups exceed the minimum (≥6). The study reports whole-brain VBM analyses (voxelwise, corrected and uncorrected thresholds) and presents results in figures/tables (coordinates likely provided in main/supplement). Core article content (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for this review and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical VBM study that includes a clearly defined subgroup of clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients and reports group-level voxelwise comparisons against healthy controls. Methods state use of voxel-based morphometry with whole-brain voxelwise analyses corrected for multiple comparisons (FWE/FDR) and figures/slices showing results. The bvFTD-specific analyses were performed on subjects with a clinical diagnosis of bvFTD (n=15 tau-positive and n=30 TDP-43-positive, and pooled bvFTD severity groups), each compared to age- and gender-matched controls, satisfying sample size requirements (>6 per group) and sample purity (bvFTD analyzed separately, not pooled with other diagnoses). The paper describes whole-brain stereotactic voxelwise results (voxel-based morphometry, corrected p-values, and image displays), meeting the coordinate/reporting requirement. No exclusion criteria were met. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria for the review: it used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) (I3) and included a clinically diagnosed bvFTD group (n=11) alongside healthy controls (n=8) (I4, I5). The paper reports group-level VBM analyses comparing disease groups and explicitly reports results for bvFTD versus controls (e.g. bvFTD minus controls—lateral orbitofrontal gyrus, BA10, p=0.000, cluster=2,478), satisfying the requirement for a direct patient-versus-control contrast (I6). The diagnostic groups were analysed separately (bvFTD not pooled with other patient groups), meeting sample purity (I7). The methods state VBM analyses with small-volume corrections and reference to coordinates (Table 1) and report stereotactic loci/BA for clusters, indicating whole-brain stereotactic reporting (I8). The full text provided includes Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion; tables are referenced though some coordinate tables may be in tables/supplementary files. Overall, the study is eligible for inclusion in the bvFTD VBM meta-analysis.

Exclusion rationale: This study is excluded because it reports region-of-interest manual volumetry rather than whole-brain voxelwise analyses (meets exclusion E6). Inclusion criteria met: I5 (sample size: patient groups and controls both exceed 6; FTD n=12, controls n=27). Inclusion criteria not met: I3 (imaging modality requirement — study did not use VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET; it used manual cortical parcellation/volumetry), I4 (sample must be clinically diagnosed bvFTD or Picks disease — the paper reports ‘FTD’ without explicit specification of behavioral-variant bvFTD), I6 (contrast must be bvFTD versus healthy controls — although an FTD vs control comparison is reported, it does not clearly identify a bvFTD group), I8 (requires whole-brain stereotactic coordinates for the patient-versus-control comparison — not provided because the study used ROI volumetry). Therefore the paper does not meet key modality and analysis requirements for inclusion.

This study used FDG-PET (I3) and included a clinically diagnosed frontal-variant FTD group (fv-FTD, corresponding to bvFTD; I4) with adequate sample sizes (18 patients, 18 controls; I5). Patient groups were reported separately (fv-FTD and SD), so the bvFTD group is not pooled with other patient groups (I7). However, the paper does not report any group-level whole-brain comparison directly contrasting the bvFTD/fv-FTD group against healthy controls (e.g., bvFTD < controls); the PET analyses presented are correlations within patient groups between fluency scores and FDG uptake. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I6 (required direct patient-versus-control group comparison) and I8 (reporting whole-brain coordinates for such a bvFTD-versus-control contrast). Full text appears complete. Conclusion: EXCLUDE because key inclusion criteria I6 and I8 are not met.

This study directly addresses bvFTD using FDG-PET (with arterial sampling) and also reports voxel-based morphometry (SPM) whole-brain analyses. The sample comprises 24 clinically diagnosed behavioural-variant FTD patients and 12 age-matched controls (both groups >6). The paper reports group-level comparisons of bvFTD subgroups versus healthy controls (repeated-measures ANOVAs, ROI PET contrasts) and voxel-based morphometry SPM comparisons (whole-brain) between patient groups and controls; coordinates are implied to be reported (supplementary information) and SPM maps/voxel extractions are described. The bvFTD group is not pooled with other dementia groups. No exclusion criteria apply (FDG tracer used; not a review; includes whole-brain analyses and control group). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, I7 and I8.

This study meets the review criteria: it uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM) as the imaging modality and reports whole-brain SPM analyses (I3, I8). The cohort includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients and the authors explicitly re-categorized patients by clinical syndrome and contrasted bvFTD against 25 healthy controls (I4, I6, I7). The total patient sample is 18 and the study reports group-level parametric analyses for bvFTD (with corrected statistics), indicating the patient-group sample meets the minimum size requirement (I5). No exclusion criteria apply (no review/meta-analysis, ROI-only, inappropriate imaging modality, or case-series issues), and the provided full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion (fulltext_incomplete=false). Therefore the paper should be included for the bvFTD meta-analysis.

This study uses manual ROI volumetry of the putamen on T1 MRI (manual tracing), not VBM, task/resting‑state fMRI, or FDG‑PET, so it does not meet the required imaging-modality inclusion (I3). It reports only region-based volumetric analyses rather than whole‑brain voxelwise results in stereotactic space (violates E6 and fails I8). Met inclusion criteria: I4 (includes clinically diagnosed FTD diagnosed by Neary criteria, i.e., behavioral-variant FTD), I5 (patient and control group sizes ≥6), I6 (reports group-level FTD vs control comparisons), and I7 (FTD group analyzed separately, not pooled). Exclusion criteria met: E6 (ROI-only analyses with no whole-brain results). Therefore the paper must be excluded from the review despite adequate sample size and group comparisons.

This study meets several inclusion criteria: it used voxel-based morphometry (I3), included a clinically diagnosed bvFTD group (I4), and the bvFTD and control groups each exceed the 6-participant threshold (I5). However, it does not report any group-level whole-brain voxelwise contrast that directly compares the bvFTD group against healthy controls (e.g., bvFTD < controls). The imaging analyses reported are correlation/voxelwise regression analyses across a mixed multi-diagnostic sample and co-atrophy/shared-effects checks; they controlled for diagnostic group membership but did not present a dedicated bvFTD-versus-control VBM comparison with stereotactic coordinates. Therefore inclusion criteria I6 (direct bvFTD vs control group-level comparison), I7 (that such a comparison be bvFTD alone, not pooled), and I8 (reporting whole-brain coordinates for that bvFTD-vs-control contrast) are not satisfied. No exclusion criteria from the provided list were triggered. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This study uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM), includes a frontotemporal dementia (FTD) patient group (n=47) and healthy controls (n=43), reports whole-brain results in MNI space, and has adequate sample sizes. However, it does not report any group-level VBM contrast that directly compares a behavioral-variant FTD (bvFTD) group against healthy controls. The imaging analyses are correlational (personality trait–VBM regressions) across a mixed diagnostic sample, and while diagnostic-group covariates were used in co-atrophy checks, no bvFTD-versus-control whole-brain contrast is presented and the bvFTD group is not isolated in an imaging contrast. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I6 (required direct bvFTD vs control group-level comparison) and I7 (bvFTD-versus-control comparison with bvFTD not pooled). No exclusion criteria from the list are met. Full text appears complete.

This study is excluded because its imaging data are structural ROI-based MRI volumetry (Freesurfer parcellation) rather than VBM, task/resting fMRI, or FDG-PET (I3 not met). It reports ROI volume comparisons (orbitofrontal, middle frontal gyrus) rather than whole-brain voxelwise results with stereotactic coordinates, so the coordinate requirement (I8) is not met and it falls under exclusion E6 (only ROI analyses with no whole-brain results). Inclusion criteria met: I4 (bvFTD patient sample), I5 (≥6 patients and ≥6 controls), I6 (group-level bvFTD vs control comparisons), I7 (bvFTD group not pooled with other diagnoses). Inclusion criteria not met: I3 (required imaging modalities) and I8 (whole-brain stereotactic coordinates). Full text appears complete for screening purposes.

This FDG-PET study does not meet the review’s key population and contrast requirements. While it uses FDG-PET (I3) and includes an FTD patient group of sufficient size (n=17, I5), it does not report a group-level comparison of a clinically-diagnosed bvFTD (behavioral-variant FTD) group against a recruited healthy control group. The paper used an internal/normative PET database for individual case comparisons and reported PET-vs-clinical diagnostic accuracy within a consecutive patient series, but did not present a whole-brain bvFTD-versus-control voxelwise group analysis or stereotactic coordinates. Therefore it fails I4 (bvFTD sample), I6 (bvFTD vs healthy control group-level contrast), I7 (cannot verify a pure bvFTD-vs-control comparison), and I8 (no whole-brain coordinates for such a contrast). Exclusion applied: E11 (clinical case series without a recruited control group/group-level patient-vs-control voxelwise analysis). Full text appears complete.

This paper reports voxel-based morphometry (VBM) analyses including a separate behavioral/dysexecutive (bvFTLD/bvFTD) subgroup (n=71) and compares cortical atrophy in that subgroup against an age-matched healthy control cohort (reported as ~42–43 controls) using independent-samples t tests. The methods state images were normalized into MNI space and the manuscript references tables of peak coordinates and whole-brain results (VBM, whole-brain analysis). All inclusion criteria are met: VBM imaging (I3); clinically diagnosed bvFTLD group present (I4); sufficient sample sizes for patient and control groups (I5); explicit group-level bvFTLD vs healthy control contrast (I6); bvFTLD group analyzed separately (I7); and whole-brain results in stereotactic space reported (I8). No exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This study reports structural MRI regional volumetry (striatal and thalamic VOIs) comparing apathetic vs non-apathetic FTD patients, not a whole-brain VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET analysis. Inclusion criterion I5 (sample size ≥6 patients) is met (N=21). However, it fails key inclusion criteria: I3 (imaging modality is not VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET), I6 (no group-level bvFTD vs healthy control comparison; the reported contrasts are within FTD subgroups), and I4 (paper reports ‘FTD’ without specifying clinically diagnosed bvFTD group for a bvFTD-vs-control contrast). Additionally, the study reports ROI-only analyses with no whole-brain results, meeting exclusion criterion E6. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).
